#1489. Spitting row mars feisty Millwall-West Ham clash

A spitting row marred the 100th Millwall-West Ham United derby and first for 14 years.

Taty Castellanos was facing trial by video after being accused of spitting on Filip Marschall during Saturday’s febrile 2-2 draw at the Den.

Millwall goalkeeper Marschall made the allegation to referee Paul Tierney, who was expected to include it in an official report that would then be assessed by the Football Association.

Spitting on an opponent is punishable with a six-match ban.

Telegraph Sport has been told West Ham striker Castellanos denies he spat on Marschall and believes he will be vindicated by video footage of the incident.

Lying little prick. Taty didn't spit ❌ pic.twitter.com/5vYxOtKqof

Millwall manager Alex Neil said after the game that fourth official Lewis Smith had confirmed a spitting accusation had been made.

Asked if he had spoken to Marschall about the claim, Neil replied: “I haven’t asked him about it. But it’s like anything else; I’m sure there’ll be footage of it, or not of it, if it didn’t happen.

“I’d be extremely surprised if Fil’s made an accusation and nothing’s happened. But that’s not really for me to deal with; I’m sure the authorities will deal with that.”

West Ham manager Nuno Espírito Santo said: “I’m aware of the allegation. I didn’t see the image; I didn’t speak with Taty. I cannot go much further on that.”

He added: “I’m going to try to look at the images.”

There were also ugly scenes at full time when players had to be separated at the end of a derby that had been at the centre of an unprecedented police operation.

There were six arrests as of 4pm on Saturday for offences including tailgating, assault on a police officer and entering or attempting to enter a stadium while intoxicated.

Eleven men were also arrested at around 7.15pm on Friday on suspicion of conspiracy to commit criminal damage.

The group, believed to be Millwall fans, were detained in the vicinity of a known West Ham supporters’ pub in Stratford.

Saturday’s fixture was subject to a five-mile dispersal zone, the largest ever for a football match in London, with officers granted special powers to stop and search people and vehicles without reasonable suspicion and to remove anyone causing disorder.

Riot police were out in force outside the ground, with dog units and mounted officers among 400 personnel deployed – roughly quadruple the usual number for a game there.

Those and other measures – including the use of live facial recognition, a strict segregation policy and a 12.30pm kick-off to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time – prevented a repeat of the kind of violence which has marred this fixture down the years.

West Ham fans also received a police escort to a game that saw both sets of supporters hurl foul-mouthed insults at each other throughout.

Plans to keep rival spectators apart after the match were reportedly tested by scuffles that broke out as people left the ground.

If the police were ready for a fight before the game, West Ham’s players were not as Millwall tore into them from the first whistle and dominated a first half in which they scored twice through Caleb Taylor and Camiel Neghli and hit the crossbar through a stunning 35-yard strike by Mark Sykes.

MILLWALL STRIKE FIRST 🔥Caleb Taylor fires the Lions in front! pic.twitter.com/pPffYZD73D

However, the Championship leaders finally turned up in the second half and pulled a goal back through Mohamadou Kanté before Konstantinos Mavropanos equalised with just 10 minutes to go.

ALL SQUARE at the Den 🙌West Ham equalise in the 80th minute.Everything to play for with just 10 minutes remaining 👀 pic.twitter.com/qQmDlyuQmT

That was only after Marschall gestured that he had been spat at by Castellanos following a melee in the penalty area.

Tierney did, though, brandish a red card when Kanté pulled back Kyrell Lisbie as the substitute robbed him of the ball on the halfway line and ran clean through on goal.

The foul denied Lisbie the chance to hand Millwall their first win over their bitter rivals for 22 years, much to the frustration of fans who had roared them on from first whistle to last.

RED CARD 🟥West Ham are down to ten men, after Kante was sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity. pic.twitter.com/jRlVwLNiOs

Describing the atmosphere as “absolutely the best by far” since he joined the club almost two years ago, Neil said: “I told the players prior to the game that this game’s a real rarity and, as a player and as a manager, it’s a privilege to be part of it.”

Millwall: Marschall; Osei-Tutu, Taylor, Cooper, Sturge; Metcalfe (Servais 81), Mazou-Sacko (Cundle 90); Sykes (Baggott 70), Dykes, Neghli; Arconte (Lisbie 81).Booked: Lisbie 90+5.Goals: Taylor 16, Neghli 45+3.Subs not used: Batth, Crocombe, Doughty, Issoufou, Kelly.West Ham United: Hermansen; Walker-Peters (Kanté 46), Mavropanos, Kilman, Morato; Bowen, Engels, Mukasa (Austbo 68), Solomon; Piroe (Pablo 46), Castellanos (Orford 90).Booked: Morato 40, Pablo 83, Kilman 86, Mavropanos 90+5.Sent off: Kanté 89.Goals: Kanté 74, Mavropanos 80.Subs not used: Ajala, Austbo, Golambeckis, Herrick, Magassa, Scarles.Referee: Paul Tierney.

🗣️ "We started to tire in the second half"Millwall manager Alex Neil shares his thoughts on this afternoon's Dockers Derby, after the Lions drew 2-2 with West Ham. pic.twitter.com/xnmubZ9NIz

🗣️ 'We were able to bounce back, but we need to look at the things we have not done so well'Nuno Espirito Santo reflects on West Ham's performance after the Hammers fought back from 2-0 down to draw with Millwall. pic.twitter.com/NM1wQVcN0o

Asked by Sky Sports for his view on the “spitting” incident, Alex Neil said: “Fil [Marschall] was saying to the referee throughout the game when that happened at that point... Obviously I’m so far away it’s hard for me to see what happened, but I wouldn’t presume that Fil would say that without cause.

“I’m sure the referee and authorities who need to deal with it will look at it and, if it warrants it, it needs dealt with and then I’m sure they will.”

Will there be one final chance? Sturge earns a throw-in on the far side and Dykes limbers up... But West Ham clear their lines and that is that. It ends two goals apiece.

Lisbie darts to the by-line but his cutback does not make it through the thicket of limbs and West Ham clear their lines.

DYKES! 😱So close to a late winner for Millwall, but his shot flies over the bar. pic.twitter.com/fQFpQBdS7j

Woah.. Kante gets his pocket picked by Lisbie on the half-way line and the West Ham goalscorer has no choice but to foul him as the last man. West Ham have a free-kick just outside the box.

RED CARD 🟥West Ham are down to ten men, after Kante was sent off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity. pic.twitter.com/jRlVwLNiOs

Mazou-Sacko has his hands all over Pablo’s back and while the Brazilian is awarded a free-kick he slams the ball to the ground feeling he had broken free. He earns a booking for his troubles and the resulting free-kick comes to nothing.

It looks like West Ham have gone to three at the back as Kante joins Mukasa and Engels in midfield. He’ll look to make late runs in behind.

This is no more than Millwall – and West Ham – deserve. Sykes’s outrageous 35-yard strike deserved a goal and Neghli makes sure justice is served on the stroke of half-time. The roar that greets the players leaving the field is deafening.

The Den is in dreamland. Millwall take a two-goal advantage into the break and Neil celebrates with unbridled delight on the touchline. A caveat, though... Millwall did spurn a 2-0 lead in their most recent match away at Middlesbrough.

"It's DREAMLAND at the Den!!"🫶🏼Millwall snatch a second goal before the break, as Neghli drills it home.An unbelievable half from the home side. pic.twitter.com/NIfSmwkHXh

WHAT A HIT!! 💥Sykes' long-range effort RATTLES the crossbar. A potential contender for goal of the season, had that gone into the net... pic.twitter.com/ivBOslIZaO

Millwall, for the umpteenth time, find themselves in a two-vs-two situation on the beak, as Arconte tries to twist Kilman one way and then the other. He sets the ball to Metcalfe but the contact is not great and Hermansen gathers.

West Ham threaten Millwall’s lead momentarily as Mukasa breaks down their right, but Marschall does well to smother the ball and earns a free-kick on the process.

There’s a muted appeal for a penalty as Mavropanos nudges Cooper to the floor, but it’s a soft contact which takes place outside of the box anyhow.

Castellanos then attempts to burst down the right but Mazou-Sacko, who has been fantastic thus far, steams in and boots the ball out of play before geeing up the crowd.

Another foul... Osei-Tutu jumps into Morato but West Ham give the free-kick straight back to their opponents.

Morato leaves a leg in as Osei-Tutu attempts to break free, perhaps in retaliation to the earlier discretion, and he earns the first booking of the match.

It’s seven-seven in the fouls contest for those wondering, the latest being a mistimed challenge on Sykes by Castellanos near the right touchline. Millwall pump another ball into the box which is not up to much.

In an attempt to get his foot on the ball, Engels has often peeled out to the right-back position, but a wild, desperate cross-field ball that goes straight to Osei-Tutu sums up West Ham’s half aptly.

A wild challenge from Metcalfe on Cooper earns West Ham a free-kick and its then Sykes’ turn to land a late tackle, this time in the right channel. The subsequent delivery finds Castellanos but he cannot direct the ball goalwards.

West Ham’s strength comes from the fluidity of their front four, but Nuno’s creators have not been able to access them. So effective has Millwall’s back-line coverage been that West Ham have only managed low-quality final-third entries.

For the first time this half, Millwall begin to retreat deep into their own half, their lines of defence merging. And while West Ham tot up a fair number of passes on the edge of the box, they ultimately cede possession and Millwall spring a counter. Arconte appears to be through but Kilman does well to recover and Dykes’ subsequent shot is charged down.

West Ham are not learning their lessons and Sturge almost pulls off a similar pass in behind for Arconte, but the linesman raises his flag on this occasion. Replays show that it was really tight.

Millwall are going man-to-man as West Ham try to build and the visitors are struggling to get out. Sturge works infield from his starting perch on the left and almost threads a through-ball in behind for Arconte to gallop on to but Kilman does well to stick in a boot.

West Ham are desperately trying to calm this game down, but the Millwall fans are making that quite the challenge. The visitors string a series of passes together before Bowen strays offside.

Millwall then burst forward, Arconte this time popping up in a dangerous position on the right but Metcalfe fires over having picked off a loose Hammers pass out from the back.

Another Dykes throw-in sparks panic in West Ham’s box. Osei-Tutu’s back-post header appears to take a deflection off Walker-Peters, but the referee awards a goal-kick.

Millwall 1 West Ham 0 (Taylor) If at first you don’t succeed, try and try again... Dykes’ long throw from the right prompts chaos on the West Ham box and although Hermansen is able to keep out efforts from Sykes and Arconte, he can’t deny Taylor from close range. Cue bedlam in the stands. A massive, massive goal.

Or not… The Den erupts! That was appalling defending from a long throw and West Ham got exactly what they deserved, with Mads Hemansen’s brilliant save failing to spare them.

MILLWALL STRIKE FIRST 🔥Caleb Taylor fires the Lions in front! pic.twitter.com/pPffYZD73D

It is all Millwall so far. They have been first to pretty much every ball and are giving West Ham no time on it at all. Konstantinos Mavropanos has just bought the visitors a breather after going down injured.

Hermansen gets caught in no-man’s land as Millwall spin in another ball from deep. It falls to the feet of Dykes but his effort does not have the requisite power to beat Kilman on the line.

Mavropanos appears to have been taken out by his own goalkeeper in the commotion and receives some on-field medical treatment.

Neil will be happy with how his side have started this match. Their intensity off the ball has forced West Ham into errors and here Sturge picks Bowen’s pocket on the halfway line before picking out Arconte in the box. He tries to squeeze a shot through Mukasa but the young midfielder does well to clear his lines.

The resulting corner comes out to Mazou-Sacko on the edge of the box but his effort sails over the bar.

Dykes and Arconte are Millwall’s attacking threats and the former wins a free-kick in the left channel. The hosts load the box with their biggest aerial threats but Metcalfe’s teasing inswinger just evades everyone. Tierney blows up for a foul anyhow...

There’s a minor clash off the ball as Morato and Cooper exchange words. Paul Tierney speaks with both players before Dykes launches a long throw into the box which is cleared and Hermansen is wise to the subsequent cross off the second phase.

Arconte tiptoes into the West Ham box and picks out Sturge whose miscued shot finds Metcalfe on the edge of the box. His effort is straight at Hermansen who collects the ball calmly.

That Jenson Metcalfe tackle on West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen came after just 15 seconds. What Vinny Jones might call “a reducer”.

"That's the expectation, I would imagine" 😅The first free-kick is awarded just 12 seconds into Millwall's derby against West Ham.Watch it LIVE on ITV1 🎥 pic.twitter.com/qpxjQEKN6x

Millwall launch a free-kick from deep into the box after Castellanos gives away a needless foul and after some pinball Hermansen gathers.

It took just 13 seconds for us to get our first foul. Kudos to anyone who had that in their Dockers Derby sweepstake... A late lunge from Metcalfe on Bowen.

And the players emerge, Hey Jude now being played... Millwall are in their customary navy-blue home strip and white shorts. West Ham are giving their new white away kit a first outing.

There’s just about enough time for the two sides to meet for quick summits before Millwall get us under way!

The atmosphere is building nicely in the ground and the players are now lined up in the tunnel, Cooper and Bowen standing shoulder to shoulder.

Seats are filling up rapidly with barely 10 minutes before kick-off, with the away end a notable exception. The home fans are making their own presence felt as The Jam’s A Town Called Malice and The Clash’s London Calling blare out over the public-address system.

"The fans are up for it, the players are up for it" 💪🏼Lyndon Dykes looks ahead to today's match, and reflects on his strong start to life as a Millwall player.Watch it LIVE on ITV1 🎥 pic.twitter.com/V9nPzbh3Ob

Kevin Nolan, West Ham’s captain, was sent off early but his team-mates defied the odds to win 2-1 thanks to goals from Carlton Cole and Winston Reid either side of a stunning Liam Trotter strike.

In Millwall’s match-day squad that day were… Harry Kane and Ryan Mason.

The last time West Ham and Millwall met, Harry Kane was a Millwall player 😅This is how that game in 2012 played out 👇 pic.twitter.com/OhtVx3caCP

This rivalry was forged in different circumstances from most derby confrontations. There is none of the religious divide of Celtic and Rangers, or the politics of Barcelona against Real Madrid, or the spat over title-winning superiority of Manchester United and Liverpool. This is a tale of proximity, an internecine feud.

“There’s no politics, no nationality, nothing like that,” says Nick Hart, who hosts the weekly podcast Achtung! Millwall. “We’re very similar people, from the same backgrounds, same communities. But it’s in the Millwall supporter’s DNA for West Ham to be the ultimate rivals. Nobody else comes into the equation. You’re brought up on this stuff. It’s your history.”

Though possibly more recent history than might be suggested by the two clubs’ early foundations. The hostility that West Ham will face at the Den is no more about dockland rivalry, north-south London disputes or strike-breaking than the animosity when Manchester United visit Anfield is caused by the building of the Manchester Ship Canal.

“It really is about the hooligan era,” says a podcaster who uses the pseudonym Former West Ham Employee on the West Ham Way podcast. “The two clubs had notorious fanbases. And they grated. It came about through vying to be the No 1, battling to see who had the hardest mob. Whenever we’ve played – or even been in close proximity – things have happened.”

Jake Cooper on making the 500th appearance of his career against West Ham today! 👏Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/lTzXOwXhxd

There have only been 18 meetings between these fierce rivals since the Second World War, but absence has certainly not made the heart grow fonder. Here are some of the feud’s most notable flashpoints.

At the 1972 testimonial in honour of Harry Cripps – the renowned Millwall hard man – police horses were sent on to the pitch after West Ham supporters entered the home section at The Den. Fighting spilt over into the streets surrounding the ground.

An even bleaker turn came in 1976, when Millwall fan Ian Pratt died in a skirmish with West Ham fans at New Cross station that led to his fall under a train.

Leaflets were later handed out in the Den’s Cold Blow Lane end with a grainy picture of Pratt and a declaration in capital letters: “A West Ham fan must die next week to avenge him.”

Millwall plundered four goals on Mothering Sunday in 2004 as Tim Cahill’s double helped them to a 4-1 victory over West Ham at the Den in an incident-filled derby.

The hosts missed a penalty and had another saved by Stephen Bywater, who was later sent off. Violence followed in the stands and the match was named “The Mothers’ Day Massacre”.

Mother's Day Massacre ⏮️A 4-1 victory over The Hammers back in 2004. pic.twitter.com/TLi7xkcVJG

A hundred West Ham and Millwall supporters clashed during a screening of England’s 2006 World Cup match against Paraguay in Canada Square, which led to 16 injuries and one hospitalisation.

The clubs’ League Cup meeting in 2009 at Upton Park was listed as Category Five by police, the most serious risk of violence, and resulted in a Millwall supporter being stabbed in Priory Road, near the ground.

The Metropolitan Police said that “planned” scuffles, which involved more than 100 fans, appeared to have been caused by fans without tickets to the game.

Just spotted one Millwall fan outside the ground in blue boxing gloves. He is also wearing what appear to be slippers, so not sure what that means…

Nuno Espirito Santo has only been through the door at West Ham for a matter of months, but he insisted he is fully aware of the significance of today’s fixture.

When asked about his perception of the rivalry, Nuno said: “Since the fixture list came out, this date has been [important], for both of the clubs. It’s special, special game. We look forward to go and compete against a good team.

“It’s a different game from all of the other games, it’s a special game, the atmosphere will be different… Steve [Potts, first-team coach and former West Ham player] has been involved in many of these games, he’s constantly speaking about how special it is for West Ham fans, so we have a lot of information and we are fully aware of the importance of the game.

On potential unrest between fans and the significant police presence, Nuno added: “What we want most is that everything goes well, both fans supporting their teams and no conflict. We have people inside the club who are taking care of that. We have to focus on our tasks.”

The gaffer on tomorrow's fixture ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/6NG6t4t4Fn

#westham on the way to #millwall via #london bridge #whufc #coyi pic.twitter.com/HrWgJ6UtJY

Riot police are very much out in force outside The Den today for the 100th competitive derby between Millwall and West Ham United and first for 14 years. Dog units and mounted officers can been seen patrolling the perimeter of the ground, with 400 personnel deployed to stop violence erupting between rival fans – roughly quadruple the usual number for a fixture here. There has been no sign of any trouble with less than an hour to go before kick-off.

The game has been scheduled for 12.30pm to minimise supporters’ pre-match drinking time, although plenty of fans have been nursing pints before entering the ground. Other measures in place include the use of live facial recognition cameras, while a dispersal order has been imposed covering a large area around the stadium. Police were also planning to escort West Ham fans from South Bermondsey station, which will also be closed to home supporters for up to an hour after full-time. The latter measure has been deemed safer than holding the 1,800 away fans back following the game.

The Millwall-West Ham derby is one of the most notorious in English football and was most recently marred by serious violence when the sides met at Upton Park for a League Cup tie back in 2009. One man was stabbed and the match itself was interrupted on three occasions by fans invading the pitch.

Alex Neil switches out goalkeeper Max Crocombe for Filip Marschall and names the returning Mathis Servais, Kyrell Lisbie and Alfie Doughty on the bench.

Alex Neil names his Lions XI 👊 pic.twitter.com/MP0N9wMatG

Just the one change from the league leaders’ last league match as Kyle Walker-Peters comes in for the injured Joel Veltman.

Today's teamsheet 📋 pic.twitter.com/EmrxYRhsPd

"We have to quiet them down" 🤫West Ham captain Jarrod Bowen is expecting a hostile atmosphere at The Den today 🗣️Watch all the action with NOW! https://t.co/56JOZ0NPsr pic.twitter.com/9tp2225Rq8

The Metropolitan Police will have 400 officers on the streets of east London for this match – about four times the norm for a Championship fixture – and it has enforced a Section 35 dispersal order in the area highlighted on the map below.

A Section 35 order authorises a Police Constable and a Police Community Support Officer in uniform to “exclude a person from an area for a period of up to 48 hours with an Inspector’s authority”.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of the highly anticipated Championship match between Millwall and West Ham United as the two clubs meet officially for the 100th time. This fixture has not been staged since 2012, and the intervening 14 years have done little to temper the ill-feeling between their passionate supporters, who will be anxious to claim bragging rights over their Dockers Derby rivals. The Metropolitan Police have placed a Section 35 dispersal order in the area surrounding The Den and will deploy 400 officers on the streets of east London.

Acrimony between the two clubs has existed since the late 19th century when Millwall Athletic, originally Rovers, battled it out against Thames Ironworks, later renamed West Ham at the Athletic and Memorial Grounds. Sixty of the two clubs’ 99 meetings came between 1899 and 1915, and while they played just seven times between 1946 and 1987, the irregularity of the game only added to its mystique, which has often spilt over into the ugly.

Both head coaches spoke at length about the significance of today’s match, with Alex Neil, in the Millwall dugout, describing it as an encounter that means “absolutely everything” but imploring his players to keep “cool heads”. His counterpart Nuno Espírito Santo revealed that he had been well advised about the game’s importance by Steve Potts, his first-team coach and former West Ham player.

Since the club’s last meeting in 2012, West Ham have ascended into the Premier League, moved into the London Stadium and won the Uefa Conference League, only falling back into England’s second tier last summer where Millwall have remained for all but two seasons. The Lions brushed maddeningly close to promotion in their last campaign as they pushed for an automatic spot until the very last weekend of the regular season before falling to Hull City in the play-off semi-finals.

Much of the pre-match talk will centre on the clubs’ long-standing rivalry, but beneath the bile and belligerence is an intriguing football match between two sides. Millwall are missing 11 first-team players and face the daunting task of stopping a West Ham side who have found their feet in the Championship, scoring 16 goals in their last four league matches.

#1487. Man Utd transfer news: Red Devils 'snubbed' by Premier League striker prior to recent contract announcement

By Carter White | 27 Nov 2026 15:20

Manchester United were reportedly snubbed by Leeds United striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin before he signed a contract extension at Elland Road.

Mauricio Pochettino's men are heading towards a full-blown relegation battle in the top flight this season, with the Red Devils sitting 19th in the Premier League table after winning one of their first 11 matches.

At the other end of the standings, Daniel Farke's Leeds are in seventh position and recently announced a contract extension for talisman Calvert-Lewin, who is now committed to the club until the summer of 2029.

Following his 2025 arrival on a free transfer from Everton, the 29-year-old has established himself as one of the best strikers in the Premier League, as well as earning call-ups to England squads under Thomas Tuchel.

Leeds are supposedly in the market for new attacking options during the winter trading point, however, there is no doubting that Calvert-Lewin will remain a first-choice option in the ranks of the Whites.

According to transfer expert Fabrizio Romano via TEAMtalk, Manchester United were keen on bringing Leeds and England star Calvert-Lewin to the Theatre of Dreams during the January transfer window.

However, with the 29-year-old since signing club-record terms at Elland Road, the report claims that the former Everton attacker snubbed the advances of the 20-time English champions.

As well as the out-of-form Red Devils, it is understood that two clubs from Italy were extremely interested in securing the services of Calvert-Lewin during the most recent summer transfer window.

Ultimately, Leeds decided to keep hold of their talent and the player opted to stay put at Elland Road, where Farke's side are looking to push on and secure European qualification this season.

It is believed that Calvert-Lewin has become the highest-paid player in Leeds history by agreeing his new terms, with the Englishman expected to be earning upwards of £110,000 per week.

In the days of Sir Alex Ferguson, plucking one of the Premier League's best strikers from a rival would be relatively simple for Manchester United - see Robin van Persie's 2012 switch from Arsenal as an example.

However, those glory days are long behind the fallen English giants, who are hurtling towards a bottom-three scrap if their form does not seriously improve under new head coach Pochettino.

All things considered, it makes complete sense that Calvert-Lewin snubbed an approach from Man Utd in order to continue building a legacy for Leeds at Elland Road.

#1486. Crystal Palace's Ismaila Sarr at centre of African Player of the Year controversy as agent demands transparency

By Naim Beneddra | 27 Nov 2026 15:21

Ismaila Sarr's agent has launched a fierce criticism of the Confederation of African Football (CAF) after the Crystal Palace winger was left off the final five-man shortlist for the 2026 African Player of the Year award, demanding that the governing body publish the full voting results.

The Senegal international enjoyed a remarkable European campaign with Palace, winning the Conference League and finishing as both the competition's leading goalscorer and its Player of the Season. He also scored four goals at the 2026 World Cup, equalling Roger Milla's African record for goals at a single edition of the tournament.

However, Sarr was overlooked in favour of Sadio Mane, Pape Gueye, Achraf Hakimi, Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari when the final shortlist was announced on Wednesday, prompting an angry response from his representative, former Premier League forward Diomansy Kamara.

Kamara, who represented Fulham, Portsmouth and West Bromwich Albion during his playing career in England, took to social media on Wednesday evening to question the credibility of the selection process.

The former Senegal international listed Sarr's achievements before demanding that CAF explain how a player with such a record could fail to make the final five.

"We demand transparency, clear criteria and the publication of the detailed voting results," Kamara wrote, before expressing his frustration with the way African football is governed.

Sarr's contribution to Palace's European success was particularly impressive. The 28-year-old scored nine goals in the Conference League, finding the net in both legs of the semi-final against Shakhtar Donetsk. His strike after just 21 seconds in the first leg also established a new record for the fastest goal in the competition's history.

Both his European triumph and his World Cup performances fell within CAF's designated assessment period, which ran from January 1 to September 15, 2026.

One possible explanation for Sarr's absence concerns the timing of the Court of Arbitration for Sport's decision to restore Senegal's Africa Cup of Nations title.

Voting for the African Player of the Year award closed on November 20, four days before Senegal were officially reinstated as African champions.

Consequently, voters submitted their selections while Morocco were still officially recognised as the tournament winners, despite Senegal having prevailed on the pitch in January's final.

Another possibility is that support for Senegal's three leading candidates was divided. Mane was named the best player at the Africa Cup of Nations, while Gueye scored the winning goal in the final. Both had strong cases, although neither could match Sarr's individual achievements in European club football and at the World Cup.

CAF has explained that the winners are determined by a voting panel drawn from several areas of African football, including national team coaches and captains, technical experts and journalists. The process is independently monitored by PricewaterhouseCoopers.

There is therefore no evidence that Sarr was deliberately excluded by the governing body. Equally, without a detailed breakdown of the votes, it is impossible to establish whether the timing of the CAS ruling or competition between Senegal's nominees materially affected his candidacy.

The winner will be announced at the CAF Awards ceremony in Lagos on December 2. For Kamara, however, the more pressing issue is establishing how one of the most productive African players in European football failed to make the final shortlist.

#1485. Manchester City favourites to sign Borussia Dortmund star after formal approach

Barnaby Lane is a highly experienced sports writer who has written for The Times, FourFourTwo Magazine, Sports Illustrated, TalkSPORT, and Business Insider. Over the years, he's had the pleasure of interviewing some of the biggest names in world sport, including Usain Bolt, Rafael Nadal, Christian Pulisic, and more.

Manchester City are continuing to invest in young talent as they look to strengthen their squad for the future, with another exciting prospect emerging on their transfer radar.

Pep Guardiola’s side have reportedly moved into pole position for one of Borussia Dortmund’s most highly rated youngsters.

United States international Mathis Albert has attracted interest from several European clubs, but City are currently considered the favourites to secure his signature.

With the teenager’s first-team opportunities limited in Germany, the Premier League champions could look to take advantage of the situation.

According to TEAMtalk, Manchester City are the frontrunners to sign Albert after making a formal approach during the summer transfer window.

The report claims City are prepared to offer the 17-year-old lucrative personal terms as they step up their pursuit. Their interest is serious, with the club previously prepared to meet a valuation in the region of €20 million (£16.7m).

Chelsea are also long-term admirers of the youngster and were reportedly willing to spend a similar amount last winter. Paris Saint-Germain previously made contact with Dortmund in 2025, while Arsenal and Liverpool have more recently been monitoring his situation.

However, City are currently viewed as being in the strongest position should Dortmund soften their stance.

Albert joined Borussia Dortmund from the LA Galaxy academy in 2024 and has quickly established himself as one of the most exciting young American talents in European football. He has already made Bundesliga appearances and earned senior international recognition with the United States.

Despite his potential, opportunities under Niko Kovac have been limited this season. That lack of regular first-team football has encouraged several clubs to monitor his development, although Dortmund remain determined to keep hold of their young attacker.

The Bundesliga side have reportedly rejected approaches, including loan enquiries, and continue to view Albert as an important part of their long-term plans. They are also preparing a contract extension offer, with his current agreement running until June 2027.

There is another important factor for City. Premier League regulations prevent English clubs from signing Albert permanently until he turns 18 in May, meaning any potential transfer would be geared towards next summer rather than an immediate move.

#1484. The two things Roberto De Zerbi demanded from Luca Williams-Barnett's first Tottenham start as 18-year-old star signs new lucrative deal, writes MATT BARLOW

Published: 08:08 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 18:17 EST, 24 November 2026

Having summoned Luca Williams-Barnett to his office to let the teenager know he would be making his first Premier League start, Roberto De Zerbi could not resist a little bit of fun.

De Zerbi cast a serious demeanour and told him he had weighed the options and figured the best course of action would be 60 minutes with the Under-21s.

Williams-Barnett did not hide his disappointment. 'Why, do you think you are ready to start for the first team?' asked the Spurs boss. The 18-year-old said he thought so.

De Zerbi cracked a smile and told him he was in the team against Ipswich but demanded two things in return.

First, that his young star would play with freedom as though 'in the park with friends' and second that he would work without the ball in the manner of the world's best players in his position, such as Lamine Yamal.

This is where the comparisons to Yamal emerged soon after Williams-Barnett lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. On Tuesday, he was rewarded for his progress with a new contract at the club.

He said: 'This is a special moment for me and my family, and one I have worked really hard to reach. But this is only the start.

Luca Williams-Barnett scored his first Premier League goal for Tottenham on his first start in the top flight

The talented academy youngster may not be lightning fast but he has pace and creates goals

'Spurs is a family to me. I've been here for so long – it's a second home, where I trust the people and coaches who have pushed me to become the player I am today.

'The club has trusted and believed in me, now I'm ready to repay that.'

Hopes are indeed high. Similarities with Yamal are evident in physique, his fluency of movement on the ball and the bursts of pace, the way they look to play. Even the hairstyle.

Just as Yamal, a left footer, likes to operate wide on the right for Barcelona and Spain, De Zerbi deployed Williams-Barnett as a right footer on the left, although most of his youth career has been spent centrally in the No 10 position.

He does not possess what you would consider in modern football to be exceptional pace, but he is quick, and his strengths are on the ball. He likes the ball. He creates. And he scores goals.

From wide on the left against Ipswich, he scored within 15 minutes, darting in at the back post to finish, and created the second for Dominic Solanke, with a 60-yard run from inside his own half and cross with his left foot.

His brilliance lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, where there has not been a lot to celebrate in the last 18 months. Terrible home form was the crux of last season's relegation fears.

Here, they rose to salute a new talent, one of their own. One De Zerbi believes has the attitude to match his outrageous talent. Confident, certainly. Aware of his natural gifts and his technical skills. Perhaps bordering on arrogance when on the pitch.

De Zerbi was pleased to see Williams-Barnett, in a seat nearby on the team bus from the training ground to the stadium, watching YouTube clips of Ronaldinho, Eden Hazard and Neymar.

The Spurs boss, who has faith in the power of inspirational video footage, took this as a positive sign. The youngster was relaxed but more than this he had a passion for football and always looking to learn.

'I'm positive about his character and behaviour because I've been working with him for three or four months and I know him enough,' said De Zerbi, whose tactical instructions involved James Maddison operating closely to Williams-Barnett, a kindred spirit in a footballing sense able to talk him through the game.

When the teenager set off on the swaggering run for Solanke's goal, Maddison could be seen nearby urging him forward into the ocean of space left open by Ipswich.

The 18-year-old had rival clubs circling but Spurs have now tied him down

Born and raised in Luton, Williams-Barnett comes from a strong, grounded family - which will only help as he looks to assimilate into the senior side

Spurs have prioritised Premier League experience in the transfer market under De Zerbi to create a more mature dressing room environment. Signings such as Andy Robertson have been key to this.

The policy is not purely for the benefit of academy graduates stepping into the first-team environment, but it does help when it comes to setting the standards required in elite sport.

Anyone gifted enough to break into the Spurs squad will have been feted as a star through the youth development phase and well rewarded to resist others trying to lure them away.

Williams-Barnett was under contract until 2028 but his new deal means clubs circling must now look elsewhere.

It is easy for impressionable teens to become conceited in this situation. Williams-Barnett has had discipline and time-keeping issues but most at Spurs speak of a young man devoted to his football from a strong, loving family who are sure to keep him grounded.

He was born and raised in Luton, starting out in Luton Town's pre-academy to Under 10s, before Spurs paid a small fee for him.

His father Jonathan Barnett was a central midfielder in Step Three of non-league football, known as 'Jono' and playing for various clubs in the region including Dunstable Town and Arlesey Town and renowned for his passing, set pieces and with an eye for goal.

Although more of a dribbler, Luca grew up with football in the family, polishing his technical skills with his dad in the back garden. 'He is from a very good family and it's crucial for this type of players,' said De Zerbi.

Spurs have been here before, of course, with talented teens breaking through with N17 at their feet.

There was Mikey Moore's wonderful cameo against AZ Alkmaar after which Ange Postecoglou called for patience and commonsense, and Maddison went on TV and said it was 'like having Neymar on the left wing'.

There was Jose Mourinho taking the match ball from Son Heung-min, who had just scored the most incredible solo goal against Burnley, and handing it to Troy Parrott on his Premier League debut.

There was Mauricio Pochettino dubbing Marcus Edwards his 'mini Messi'. Pochettino soon came to wish he had not burdened Edwards with such lavish praise.

The pitfalls are well known and progress is rarely a smooth upward trajectory. It is a balancing act between maximising potential and getting carried away.

De Zerbi is quietly confident Williams-Barnett has what it takes to handle the hype.

On the new deal, thought to be for five years, the manager said: 'Luca is a player I think the world of, and I'm so happy that he has signed a new contract.

'He has benefitted from being around the first team every day, growing in stature and consistency, and has deserved his place in the matchday squad over recent weeks.

'Everyone can see how technically gifted Luca is on the pitch but I also love his calmness and decision-making under pressure.

'The best players have confidence on the pitch and humility off it. There is still plenty of room for Luca to improve, and I know he will continue to work hard every day to be the best version of himself.'

#1483. Man City owners facing fresh pressure as three Premier League rivals call for forced sale

By Naim Beneddra | 27 Nov 2026 15:42

The owners of Manchester City are facing renewed scrutiny after senior figures at three Premier League clubs reportedly called for them to be forced to sell the club in the wake of its financial breaches.

An independent commission found City guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League, relating to alleged breaches of financial regulations between 2009 and 2018. The club denies wrongdoing and has appealed against the verdict, with sanctions yet to be determined.

While much of the debate has centred on potential points deductions, financial penalties and the possible removal of titles, some of City's domestic rivals believe that a change of ownership would be necessary to restore confidence in the competition.

Should Man City's owners be forced to sell up as punishment for breaking financial rules? ? https://t.co/YfIws1lvS6

According to BBC Sport, senior figures at three Premier League clubs have privately expressed their belief that City's Abu Dhabi owners should be compelled to relinquish control of the club.

One executive, speaking anonymously, suggested that any punishment would be inadequate if the current ownership remained in place, while also questioning the purpose of clubs funding an independent regulator if it was unwilling to intervene in such circumstances.

The independent commission found that City had inflated revenues and concealed losses amounting to approximately £900m through commercial arrangements deemed illegitimate. The findings cover nine seasons, during which City won three Premier League titles.

City strongly dispute those conclusions, arguing that the commission's decision contains fundamental errors of law and fact. Their appeal hearing is expected to take place in December, with a verdict anticipated in the new year.

The latest intervention from rival executives represents a significant development in the wider dispute. Even if City were handed a substantial points deduction or a financial penalty, those measures would not necessarily affect Sheikh Mansour's control of the club.

However, the power to enforce a change of ownership rests with the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), whose responsibilities extend beyond the Premier League's disciplinary framework.

Speaking before a parliamentary committee on Wednesday, IFR chairman David Kogan made it clear that the regulator would not be deterred by the prospect of taking action against one of England's most successful clubs.

"We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.

The Football Governance Act 2025 gives the regulator extensive powers over club ownership. Under Section 34, the IFR can assess whether existing owners continue to satisfy suitability requirements, including standards of honesty, integrity and financial soundness.

Should an owner be deemed unsuitable, Section 39 provides a mechanism through which the regulator can require them to relinquish their ownership within a specified period. Section 43 also allows the IFR to issue an ownership removal order and appoint independent trustees to oversee the process where the relevant legal conditions are met.

Such intervention would require a separate assessment of the individuals concerned. An unsuccessful appeal by Manchester City would not, in itself, automatically trigger a sale of the club.

The regulator's independence is particularly significant given Sheikh Mansour's position as vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates, alongside the country's extensive economic interests in the United Kingdom.

However, Kogan has insisted that political considerations will have no bearing on the regulator's assessment of the evidence.

For now, the immediate focus remains on City's appeal against the independent commission's findings. Should the verdict be upheld, the club could find themselves facing two separate proceedings: one determining the sporting consequences of the financial breaches and another examining whether the individuals responsible for running the club remain suitable owners and directors.

#1482. Gallery: ‘Back in the hunt’, ‘The Devil wears Hutchinson’ – Today’s front pages in Italy

AC Milan produced a stunning second-half comeback to beat Olympiacos 4-2 and boost their chances of reaching the Europa League knockout stage.

After 50 minutes in Greece it looked like being another miserable European night for Milan, who trailed through a Mike Maignan own-goal and a strike from Jota Silva. However, Omari Hutchinson inspired a comeback, scoring after a solo run then setting up Alphadjo Cisse and Christian Pulisic.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Diego Moreira finished off a counter-attack in the closing seconds to make sure of the three points, which boost the Rossoneri back into the top 24 with three games to go.

Below are how the sports newspapers in Italy look, with each of them mentioning Milan’s comeback in Piraeus.

La Gazzetta dello Sport: “Comeback. Milan rally and gets back in the hunt. Trailing by two goals, the Rossoneri win in Athens (4-2), inspired by Hutchinson. Amorim eyes the play-offs.”

Corriere dello Sport: “Milan’s time. They turn the tables on Olympiacos: coming back from 0-2 to win 4-2 in just 39 minutes. A nightmarish start in Piraeus, but the Englishman Hutchinson proved decisive with his moments of brilliance: a goal and two assists. Cissé (his 10th goal of the season), Pulisic, and Moreira also got on the scoresheet. Amorim’s side now sit in 20th place, within the play-off zone.”

Tuttosport: “The Devil wears Hutchinson. From 0-2 down to a 4-2 win against Olympiacos: the Englishman orchestrates the turnaround. A big-club response from Milan following a horrific first 50 minutes.

“The playmaker scores with a spectacular coast-to-coast run, provides assists for Cissé and Pulisic, and finally launches the counter-attack finished off by Moreira. Amorim finds a glimmer of light in Europe, too: ‘It’s the beginning of something’.”

QS: “A comeback for the Diavolo. Amorim, a display of play-off-worthy pride. In the Europa League, after falling two goals behind, Milan fought back, unleashing a lethal four-goal salvo – courtesy of Hutchinson, Cisse, Pulisic, and Moreira – to overwhelm Olympiacos and put the Rossoneri back in the hunt for a spot in the round of 16.”

#1481. Barcelona targeting January move for Tottenham Hotspur defender

Barnaby Lane is a highly experienced sports writer who has written for The Times, FourFourTwo Magazine, Sports Illustrated, TalkSPORT, and Business Insider. Over the years, he's had the pleasure of interviewing some of the biggest names in world sport, including Usain Bolt, Rafael Nadal, Christian Pulisic, and more.

Tottenham could face growing interest in one of their key players ahead of the January transfer window, with Barcelona president Joan Laporta reportedly keen on bringing Pedro Porro to the Nou Camp.

The Spanish right-back has attracted attention following his performances for Spain at the World Cup, but Spurs have several reasons to feel confident about keeping hold of the defender.

According to Catalan broadcaster 3Cat, Porro is one of Laporta’s preferred defensive targets as Barcelona consider whether to strengthen their backline in January.

The Catalan club have been dealing with a series of defensive injuries involving Eric Garcia, Jules Kounde, Andreas Christensen and Xavi Espart. However, Barcelona have not made a final decision on whether to bring in another defender, with the club waiting to assess the injured players’ recoveries.

Laporta’s admiration for Porro reportedly grew during Spain’s World Cup campaign. The Tottenham defender became an important part of the national team, developing a strong understanding with Lamine Yamal on the right flank and scoring twice during the tournament, including in the semi-final against France.

Laporta watched that semi-final in Dallas and was reportedly impressed by Porro’s performance. Barcelona had also gathered information about the defender towards the end of the previous summer transfer window, but their enquiry did not progress into a formal proposal to either the player or Tottenham.

Porro’s contractual situation gives Spurs a strong negotiating position. The 27-year-old renewed his contract shortly before the World Cup, committing his future to the north London club until 2031.

Reports have also indicated that Tottenham would demand a significant fee to consider allowing the defender to leave. Real Madrid have also been linked with an interest in the Spain international, potentially creating further competition for his signature.

Barcelona’s admiration for Porro is a reminder of the defender’s standing in European football, but there is currently no confirmed bid or formal approach.

Tottenham will be keen to retain a player who remains an important part of their plans. His long-term contract also means the club are under no immediate pressure to negotiate a sale.

The situation could develop if Barcelona decide their defensive injury problems require January reinforcements. For now, however, Spurs remain in a strong position, and any interested club would likely have to make a substantial offer to test their resolve.
